text: PITFALL: Samples were sequenced on three MSK-IMPACT panel versions (IMPACT341 n~214, IMPACT410 n~911, IMPACT468 n~9). A gene missing from an older panel has zero mutations by construction, so using all samples as the denominator understates its frequency. If panel version differs by side, this can also bias a side comparison. CHECK: confirm each of the six genes is targeted on every panel version used (e.g. any RNF43 or AKT1 calls in IMPACT341 samples?), and cross-tabulate GENE_PANEL against PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION. IF FOUND: restrict each gene's denominator to samples whose panel covers it, or adjust for panel in logistic regression. SOURCE: https://doctors.anticancer.co.il/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/MSK-IMPACT.pdf

label: One sample per patient
text: PITFALL: Some patients have more than one tumour sample (about 31 patient IDs repeat in data_clinical_sample.txt). Counting samples instead of patients double-counts concordant driver mutations and breaks the independence that Fisher/chi-square tests assume. CHECK: count unique PATIENT_ID compared with SAMPLE_ID within the analysed MSS left/right set. IF FOUND: keep one sample per patient (e.g. prefer the primary, or the first/highest-coverage sample), or collapse to patient level (altered in any sample). KRAS/NRAS/BRAF are almost always concordant between primary and metastasis, but SMAD4 is less concordant. SOURCE: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13059-014-0454-7

label: Define FN/FP by SV fusion, not histology
text: PITFALL: Using Oncotree histology (ARMS vs ERMS) as a stand-in for fusion status misclassifies tumors, because a sizeable share of alveolar RMS (about 20-40%) are PAX-FOXO1 fusion-negative and behave like ERMS; FN-RMS/FP-RMS are defined by the fusion. CHECK: In data_sv.txt, find PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 (also PAX3/PAX7 with other partners) per patient (any sample), and cross-tabulate with ONCOTREE_CODE ARMS/ERMS. IF FOUND: Group patients by fusion detected in any of their samples (FP) vs none (FN); treat histology only as a fallback and report any ARMS-without-fusion cases explicitly. SOURCE: https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2009.26.3814 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9425116/

label: Sidedness definition
text: PITFALL: Sidedness definitions vary. Most studies call proximal to the splenic flexure (cecum, ascending, hepatic flexure, transverse) right, and splenic flexure, descending, sigmoid and rectum left. Transverse colon is ambiguous, and including or excluding rectum changes frequencies. CHECK: cross-tabulate PRIMARY_SITE against PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION (Left/Right/NA). Look at how transverse colon and rectum are assigned, and how many samples are NA. IF FOUND: use the provided PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION as the primary analysis, exclude NA, and run a sensitivity analysis that drops transverse colon (and optionally analyses rectum separately). SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.6004/jnccn.2017.0038 ; https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/24/5/1062/81237/Classifying-Colorectal-Cancer-by-Tumor-Location

label: Acquired alterations need paired, ordered samples
text: PITFALL: 'Acquired/new' alterations require a within-patient earlier vs later comparison; SAMPLE_TYPE (Primary/Metastasis/Local Recurrence) is not chronology, and a 'Primary' can be sequenced after a metastasis (e.g. T03 primary after T02 met). CHECK: Keep only patients with >=2 tumor samples; order samples by sample suffix (T01<T02<...) and by Primary-vs-later type, and flag patients where the two disagree or where several later samples exist. IF FOUND: Define new alterations as present in the later sample(s) but absent in the earliest sample of the same patient; run a sensitivity analysis with the alternate ordering; do not count alterations of single-sample patients as 'new'. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.31184

label: Panel-version mismatch inflates new alterations
text: PITFALL: Paired samples were sequenced on different MSK-IMPACT versions (IMPACT410, 468, 505); an alteration in a gene covered only by the later, larger panel looks 'acquired' though the earlier panel could not detect it. CHECK: Use data_gene_panel_matrix.txt per sample and the panel gene lists; for each pair, count how many 'new' alterations fall in genes absent from the earlier sample's panel. IF FOUND: Count acquired alterations only in genes covered by both samples' panels (intersection); compare FN vs FP on this harmonized count. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9103036/ ; https://github.com/cBioPortal/datahub/issues/1835

label: Purity differences create fake private mutations
text: PITFALL: Low tumor purity or coverage in one sample of a pair causes false negatives, so mutations look private/new (or lost) when they are actually shared. CHECK: Compare TUMOR_PURITY and SAMPLE_COVERAGE between paired samples; for each 'new' mutation look at t_alt_count/t_depth (VAF) and whether the earlier sample had a low purity (<=30%). IF FOUND: Treat low-VAF new mutations in pairs with a low-purity earlier sample as uncertain; report counts with and without them and check whether the FN vs FP difference persists. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10154864/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9816983/

label: RNF43 G659fs MSI artefact
text: PITFALL: RNF43 p.G659fs (and R117fs) sit in mononucleotide repeats and are typical of MSI tumours. In MSS CRC, RNF43 mutation tracks BRAF-mutant serrated (mostly right-sided) tumours. Residual MSI or indeterminate samples, or unfiltered repeat-indels, therefore create a spurious right-sided RNF43 enrichment. CHECK: after the MSS filter, list RNF43 variants by HGVSp and check how many are G659fs or R117fs and what MSI_SCORE/TMB those samples have. IF FOUND: drop samples with indeterminate MSI scores or high TMB, and report RNF43 with and without G659fs. Treat the RNF43 result as partly downstream of BRAF status. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5342576/ ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-022-01976-z

label: CNA calls purity-dependent; count types separately
text: PITFALL: Discrete CNA calls (-2..2 in data_cna.txt) depend on purity and thresholds, so a gene called amplified/deleted in only one sample of a pair may reflect purity, not a new event; also 'alterations' includes CNAs and SVs, not only mutations. CHECK: Count new mutations, new CNAs (only +/-2, high-level) and new SVs separately per pair, and check whether new CNAs cluster in low-purity earlier samples; use the .seg log-ratios to confirm. IF FOUND: Base the main conclusion on mutations plus high-level CNAs/SVs, and state whether the FN<FP direction holds for each alteration type. SOURCE: https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(22)00103-9/fulltext

label: Small n and outliers: per-patient counts
text: PITFALL: With a handful of paired patients per group, one hypermutated or highly altered relapse (e.g. after alkylating chemotherapy) can dominate total counts and flip which group 'acquires more'. CHECK: Tabulate new-alteration counts per patient (not pooled totals) for FN and FP, look for outliers, check TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS of later samples. IF FOUND: Compare per-patient medians (Mann-Whitney / permutation test), report results with and without outliers; acknowledge low power, judge direction and consistency rather than only p-values. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1775-1 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10066020/

label: Define 'no common mutations' before testing
text: PITFALL: 'No common mutations' is ambiguous: it can mean no shared (truncal) mutations between primary and relapse within a patient, or no gene recurrently acquired across FN patients. CHECK: Compute both: (a) per FN patient, mutations shared by early and later samples; (b) genes acquired in >=2 FN patients versus genes recurrently acquired in FP patients. IF FOUND: State which reading the evidence addresses; the hypothesis is most naturally the across-patient reading (no recurrently acquired gene in FN-RMS), and both parts (fewer new alterations AND no recurrent acquired mutation) must hold for 'True'. SOURCE: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.05369

label: Per-gene vs composite test and multiplicity
text: PITFALL: The hypothesis names six genes jointly. Prior literature in MSS CRC shows right-sided enrichment for KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, AKT1, RNF43 and SMAD4, and left-sided enrichment for TP53, APC and EGFR-pathway amplifications. Analysts can wrongly reject the claim because one gene is non-significant (e.g. AKT1 is rare and underpowered), or wrongly accept it by pooling into one 'any of six' test that is driven by KRAS/BRAF alone. CHECK: run a per-gene Fisher exact test (right vs left) with odds ratio, 95% CI and BH-FDR across the six genes. Report direction for each gene, and also a pooled any-alteration comparison. IF FOUND: judge the hypothesis on direction consistency plus FDR-significant enrichment in most genes. Do not call it False just because a rare gene like AKT1 is non-significant with the same direction. Call it False only if genes show significant left-sided enrichment or clearly null effects in the major genes. SOURCE: https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/24/5/1062/81237/Classifying-Colorectal-Cancer-by-Tumor-Location

label: Include CNA/SV as alterations
text: PITFALL: 'Oncogenic alterations' can include copy-number and structural events, not only mutations. SMAD4 homozygous deletion (data_cna.txt value -2) and AKT1/PIK3CA amplification or fusions in data_sv.txt add carriers. Ignoring CNA can understate SMAD4, and counting shallow losses (-1) adds noise. CHECK: count SMAD4 -2 and KRAS/PIK3CA/AKT1 +2 calls in data_cna.txt within the MSS left/right set, and check SV rows for the six genes. IF FOUND: add only deep deletions (-2) for tumour suppressors (SMAD4, RNF43) and high-level amplifications (+2) for oncogenes, as cBioPortal's DRIVER definition does. Report results with mutation-only and mutation+CNA. SOURCE: https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/oql/

label: Frequency is not significance
text: PITFALL: Calling a pathway 'significantly mutated' (or not) from the raw count/percentage of samples with a mutation in its genes, without a background expectation; large pathways with long genes are mutated in many samples by chance alone. CHECK: compute expected number of mutated samples per pathway from the cohort's per-sample mutation rate (e.g. TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS or MAF counts) times the summed coding length of pathway genes, and compare observed vs expected (binomial/Poisson per sample, combined across samples). IF FOUND: base the verdict on observed-vs-expected (PathScan/SLAPenrich-style test or dNdScv gene-set dN/dS), and report the raw frequency only as description. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/

label: Gene length bias in pathway genes
text: PITFALL: Cancer/signalling pathways (ErbB, PI3K) are enriched for long genes (e.g. ERBB4, PIK3C2G-type genes), so they collect passenger mutations in proportion to length, inflating apparent pathway mutation. CHECK: list which pathway genes carry the hits and whether they are long genes with scattered missense mutations versus known hotspots (PIK3CA E542/E545/H1047, ERBB2/ERBB3 hotspots, PTEN truncations). IF FOUND: weight expectations by gene length (PathScan) or use synonymous mutations as a neutral baseline (dN/dS); give hotspot/truncating driver hits more weight than scattered missense in long genes. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4788956/

label: Hypermutated samples dominate counts
text: PITFALL: One or a few hypermutated samples contribute most pathway mutations and can make a pathway look significantly mutated at the mutation level. CHECK: inspect the TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS distribution in data_clinical_sample.txt and mutations per Tumor_Sample_Barcode; see which samples carry the ERBB/PI3K hits. IF FOUND: count at the sample level (sample altered yes/no, as SLAPenrich/PathScan do) with per-sample background rates, and repeat the test excluding hypermutators as a sensitivity analysis. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5928049/

label: Pathway gene-set definition changes result
text: PITFALL: 'ERBB-PI3K pathway' has no single definition; KEGG ErbB signalling has ~85 genes, while TCGA PanCanAtlas curated PI3K (PIK3CA, PIK3R1, PTEN, AKT1-3, MTOR, TSC1/2, etc.) and RTK sets (EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4) are much smaller; bigger sets mean more chance hits and different conclusions. CHECK: prespecify the gene list (ideally ERBB1-4 receptors plus core PI3K/AKT/mTOR genes per Sanchez-Vega 2018) and rerun with an alternative (KEGG) list. IF FOUND (verdict flips by definition): report that and favour the curated driver-focused list, noting the dependence in reasoning. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/

label: Variant class filtering
text: PITFALL: Counting all MAF rows (Silent, Intron, UTR, Flank, RNA) as pathway mutations inflates the pathway rate; standard tools (maftools) count only non-synonymous classes. CHECK: tabulate Variant_Classification; restrict to Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift_Del/Ins, In_Frame_Del/Ins, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site, Nonstop. IF FOUND: use the non-synonymous set for the pathway test and keep Silent mutations as the neutral background (dN/dS). SOURCE: https://bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/maftools/inst/doc/maftools.html

label: Small cohort: use genesetdnds
text: PITFALL: In small cohorts (this one has 56 samples) fitting a selection/background model only on the pathway genes is unstable. CHECK: number of mutations in the pathway genes (few dozen or fewer means unstable). IF FOUND: use dNdScv's genesetdnds (fits substitution model on whole exome, then estimates dN/dS for the gene set) or a whole-exome per-sample rate; a gene-set dN/dS CI excluding 1 indicates selection, i.e. significantly mutated. SOURCE: https://github.com/im3sanger/dndscv/blob/master/R/genesetdnds.R

text: Before any modelling, establish whether the data actually contain the variables this hypothesis needs: a VTE event indicator, VTE/follow-up time, and an anticoagulation exposure. Grep every column header and every '#' description line in all six files for terms such as VTE, thrombosis, embolism, anticoagulant, heparin, DOAC, apixaban, follow-up/time, and ctDNA. Do not build proxies for exposure or outcome from genomic files (mutation counts, TMB, cancer type, CNA); a proxy is not a measurement of VTE or anticoagulation.

label: Low power: non-significance vs absence
text: PITFALL: Most cancer genes are mutated at 2-20% and small cohorts lack power; a non-significant test is weak evidence, while a pathway hit in a sizeable fraction of samples with clear drivers is strong evidence. CHECK: report the fraction of samples with a non-synonymous pathway mutation with a 95% CI, the observed/expected ratio, and the p-value; note whether hits are recurrent drivers. IF FOUND (e.g. a clear excess over background or a sizeable fraction of samples hit by known driver mutations): treat that as contradicting 'not significantly mutated'; if observed is close to expected, that supports it. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4048962/

In cfDNA panel data (e.g. MSK-ACCESS / ACCESS129 in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt), deriving it as 'has any somatic call in data_mutations' mixes up assay detection limits, clonal hematopoiesis and panel coverage. label: Sample ID mismatch / zero-mutation denominator
text: PITFALL: Wrong denominator: samples with no mutations do not appear in the MAF, and MAF Tumor_Sample_Barcode may be formatted differently from clinical SAMPLE_ID (here the MAF shows e.g. 'NPC015D' while clinical shows 'NPC15F'), so naive joins drop samples. CHECK: compare the set of MAF barcodes to clinical SAMPLE_IDs (56 samples, 1 per patient) and count matches. IF FOUND: harmonise IDs (e.g. strip zero padding / suffix) or use the clinical sample count as the denominator; never use only the samples present in the MAF. SOURCE: https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/

label: Multiple testing across pathways
text: PITFALL: If the analyst scans many pathways (maftools OncogenicPathways, KEGG) and then judges ERBB-PI3K, raw p-values are miscalibrated; conversely a single prespecified pathway does not need genome-wide correction. CHECK: note whether the ERBB-PI3K test was prespecified or picked from a scan. IF FOUND (scan): apply BH FDR across the tested pathways and report the q-value. SOURCE: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10415324

reason: This sets what counts as evidence for or against a 'does not benefit' claim, which a naive subgroup test gets wrong.
text: If exposure and outcome are present: 'no benefit in ctDNA-' cannot be concluded from a non-significant result in the ctDNA- subgroup alone. ctDNA- patients have few VTE events, so that test has little power. Count events in each ctDNA x anticoagulation cell. Report the hazard ratio with its 95% CI. Formally test the anticoagulation-by-ctDNA interaction in one model, rather than comparing subgroup p-values. Supporting 'no benefit' needs a CI that excludes a meaningful benefit, or a clear interaction.

reason: Each of these biases can create or hide an apparent anticoagulation effect in observational data.
text: If time-to-event VTE and anticoagulation data are present, address three biases. (1) Death is a competing risk: tabulate deaths before VTE and use cumulative incidence / Fine-Gray rather than 1-KM. (2) Immortal time: if anticoagulation starts after cohort entry, model it as time-varying or use a landmark analysis. (3) Confounding by indication: compare cancer type, stage and prior VTE between treated and untreated patients, and adjust for them (multivariable or propensity/IPTW).

reason: The choice of label depends on whether a variable that defines the subtype exists in these tables. The teams need to know which kind of variable defines a subtype before they choose what to analyse.
text: SCLC subtypes (SCLC-A, SCLC-N, SCLC-P, and SCLC-Y) are defined by RNA or protein (IHC) expression levels of the transcription factors ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3 (and YAP1). DNA mutations or copy-number changes do not define them. Before analysing, search every file, including the commented clinical headers, for any expression, IHC or subtype variable (e.g. grep -i 'ASCL1|NEUROD1|POU2F3|YAP1|SUBTYPE|EXPRESSION|IHC'). Then base the label on what variables actually exist and what they show.

reason: This prevents a common mistake: reading 'no calls' as 'subtype not present'.
text: If ASCL1, NEUROD1 or POU2F3 has no mutations or CNAs, that does not mean the subtype is absent, because subtype depends on expression level and not on alterations. These genes may also not be on the MSK-IMPACT panels used. Use data_gene_panel_matrix.txt, the row names in data_cna.txt and Hugo_Symbol in data_mutations.txt to check whether each gene was measured at all. A gene that was not measured counts as unmeasured, not as absent.

reason: The CNA data make proxy-based subtype inference tempting, and these proxies are unreliable.
text: Genomic proxies such as MYC amplification (linked to SCLC-N) or MYCL amplification (linked to SCLC-A) are statistical associations, not subtype definitions. For example, MYC amplification also occurs in SCLC-P/Y. SCLC is genetically homogeneous (near-universal TP53/RB1 loss), and studies have found no DNA-defined subtypes. If you look at these proxies, report them only as indirect hints and do not base the label on them.

reason: A naive search for CALR mutations can return zero and wrongly support the hypothesis.
text: CALR driver mutations in MPN are exon 9 insertions/deletions that shift the reading frame (type 1 = 52-bp deletion, p.L367fs; type 2 = 5-bp TTGTC insertion, p.K385fs; plus many other +1 frameshift indels). They are not SNVs. If you filter for missense changes or one HGVS string, you will miss them. Select every Hugo_Symbol == CALR row and tabulate Variant_Classification (Frame_Shift_Del/Ins, In_Frame_Del, ...), Start_Position (GRCh37 chr19 around 13,054,5xx) and HGVSp_Short.

reason: This decides which CALR calls count as the 'somatic CALR mutations' the hypothesis is about.
text: Not every CALR variant is a driver. Only somatic +1 frameshift indels in exon 9 that change the C-terminus are pathogenic. In-frame exon 9 deletions and point mutations may be non-functional or germline polymorphisms. Classify each CALR row: frameshift or in-frame, and check somatic status (Mutation_Status, normal alt counts) if those columns exist. Base the conclusion on somatic frameshift CALR mutations, and report other CALR variants separately.

reason: The definition of the JAK2-nonmutated group changes who counts toward the hypothesis.
text: 'JAK2 nonmutated' does not mean 'no JAK2 V617F'. JAK2 exon 12 mutations (e.g. N542-E543del, K539L) and other JAK2 drivers also make a patient JAK2-mutated. List every JAK2 row by HGVSp_Short and Variant_Classification. Use 'no JAK2 driver' as the main definition and report the stricter 'no JAK2 mutation of any kind' too.

reason: Patients with both mutations must not be counted as JAK2-nonmutated, and low-VAF JAK2 calls should be tested for their effect on the result.

Also report Uno's C truncated at a fixed horizon such as 5 years, because Harrell's C depends on the censoring pattern. If the CI of the difference includes 0, superiority is not shown.

reason: This is the operational definition the hypothesis depends on. Without it a team may treat co-occurrence of fusions and deletions as evidence of chromoplexy.
text: Chromoplexy (Baca et al. 2013, ChainFinder) is defined as chains of rearrangements whose breakpoints join one another, often across several chromosomes. It is inferred from a graph of paired breakpoints (nodes) linked by deletion bridges (edges), tested against a null model in which rearrangements occur independently and per-sample breakpoint density is accounted for. Several alterations occurring in the same tumour, or recurring together across tumours, do not show that they are interdependent. Testing chaining needs breakpoint coordinates (chromosome, position, orientation) for each rearrangement, plus a permutation or null test. Before choosing a method, check which columns data_sv.txt actually has and how many rows each sample has.

reason: Without a background model, large pathways with long genes look mutated by chance alone. This is the main methodological choice for this hypothesis.
text: Whether a pathway is 'significantly mutated' must be judged against a background expectation, not from the raw percentage of samples with a hit. Estimate the expected number of mutated samples from each sample's mutation rate (TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS or MAF counts) multiplied by the summed coding length of the pathway genes. Compare observed with expected (PathScan/SLAPenrich-style), or use synonymous mutations as the baseline (gene-set dN/dS). Long genes such as ERBB4 collect passenger mutations, so list which genes carry the hits. Check whether the hits are known hotspots or truncations (PIK3CA E542/E545/H1047, ERBB2/ERBB3 hotspots, PTEN truncations) or scattered missense mutations in long genes.

reason: The hypothesis is restricted to MSS tumours. How the MSS cohort is defined can create or remove a right-sided enrichment artefact.
text: MSI_STATUS in data_clinical_sample.txt is missing (NA) for roughly 327 of 1134 samples. Filtering on MSI_STATUS=='MSS' alone drops many MSS tumours, and keeping the NA rows lets MSI-H tumours in. MSI-H tumours are hypermutated and more common in right-sided primaries, so they can inflate right-sided mutation rates. Tabulate MSI_STATUS against MSI_SCORE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS. Define MSS as MSI_STATUS=='MSS', or as MSI_SCORE<3 when status is NA (MSIsensor: >=10 is MSI-H, 3-10 is indeterminate). Exclude MSI-H and Inconclusive samples. Run a sensitivity analysis with and without the indeterminate scores, and confirm that no hypermutated (very high TMB) samples remain.

reason: The grouping variable has to be defined consistently, and it should be checked for robustness.
text: Definitions of sidedness vary. Right is usually cecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure and transverse colon. Left is splenic flexure, descending colon, sigmoid and rectum. Transverse colon is ambiguous, and including rectum changes the frequencies. Cross-tabulate PRIMARY_SITE against PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION. Use the provided PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION (Left/Right) as the primary analysis and exclude NA. Run a sensitivity analysis that drops transverse colon, and optionally one that treats rectum separately.

Compare 'all non-silent' against 'putative driver' as a sensitivity analysis.

Drop indeterminate-MSI or high-TMB samples, and report RNF43 with and without G659fs. RNF43 status is also correlated with BRAF status, so it is not an independent signal.

reason: Double-counting patients breaks the independence assumption of the tests.
text: About 31 patient IDs have more than one sample in data_clinical_sample.txt. Within the analysed set, count unique PATIENT_ID against SAMPLE_ID. Keep one sample per patient (e.g. prefer the primary) or collapse to patient level, so that Fisher/chi-square tests are not run on non-independent observations.

reason: This sets a sound decision rule for a hypothesis that covers several genes jointly.
text: The hypothesis names six genes together. For each gene, run a right-vs-left test (Fisher exact, with odds ratio, 95% CI and BH-FDR across the six genes) and report its direction. Also report a pooled any-of-six comparison, but note that a pooled test can be driven by one or two common genes. Weigh the verdict on direction consistency and significance across the genes. Do not reject because one rare, underpowered gene is non-significant but points the same way. Do not accept on the pooled test alone.

text: FINDING: GC-rich promoters near the TSS are systematically under-covered even in whole cancer genomes (PCAWG coverage analysis, Rheinbay group), and standard WES covers them poorly (e.g. the TERT promoter is 'poorly covered by WES' and needed separate targeted sequencing; GC-rich exome regions are cold-spots behind CCLE/COSMIC discordance). FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What thresholds on segment mean log2 ratio are conventionally used to call gains and losses from exome-derived segmentation, and should they be adjusted per sample for noise or ploidy? ANSWER: No single standard exists. (1) GISTIC2 default noise thresholds are -ta/-td = 0.1, so |log2| > 0.1 counts as gain or loss. Broad Firehose/TCGA runs use 0.1, and some (e.g. low-pass) runs use 0.3. (2) CNVkit 'call -m threshold' defaults to -1.1 / -0.25 / 0.2 / 0.7: deep deletion < -1.1, loss < -0.25, gain >= 0.2, amplification >= 0.7. These are set to work down to about 50% purity and favour sensitivity. (3) For genemetrics, the CNVkit docs suggest 0.1 or 0.2 if you will filter downstream, otherwise 0.3. In a pure diploid sample a single-copy gain is +0.585 and a single-copy loss is -1.0. Purity, ploidy and subclonality shrink these values toward 0. On adjustment: tool authors and teaching material say thresholds should depend on the sample. CNVkit's author advises rescaling with --purity/--ploidy (clonal method), or moving the cutoffs closer to 0 when purity is low or unknown, plus filtering segments by confidence interval (segmetrics --ci, call --filter ci). GISTIC sets its high-level thresholds per sample from arm-level median copy number, which approximates hemizygous level given purity and ploidy. The CRUK copy-number lecture describes per-sample thresholds based on each sample's variability. So 0.1/0.2/0.3 are all defensible conventions (0.1 is GISTIC's default, about 0.2-0.25 is CNVkit's). A comparison that ties or flips across them is threshold-sensitive and should not be read as a clear difference unless per-sample noise or purity is accounted for. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://broadinstitute.github.io/gistic2/, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://www.biostars.org/p/242323/, https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/34704/how-copy-number-variation-thresholds-are-defined-in-gistic, https://bioinformatics-core-shared-training.github.io/cruk-summer-school-2017/Day2/copy_number_lecture.pdf.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the cBioPortal mutation data format, which fields indicate somatic versus germline status and allele fraction? The presence of the variants is therefore established only as the study's reported calls, not as independently confirmed somatic events. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For a hypothesis that combines a testable presence claim with an untestable functional-effect claim, how do common evaluation conventions for data-driven hypothesis verification assign a support / contradict / not-verifiable label? ANSWER: In FEVER-style verification, SUPPORTED and REFUTED both need evidence for the claim; anything else is NOT ENOUGH INFO. Under the closed-world rule, a claim is accepted only if every asserted part is supported. For a compound claim: (a) if any testable part is contradicted, e.g. the named variants are absent, the label is Refuted/False. (b) If the presence part is supported but no variable in the data bears on the functional or activation part, the claim is not Supported. It is not Refuted either, so the label is NOT ENOUGH INFO, which maps to 'Not verifiable'. One paper (arXiv 2604.10990) calls accepting a claim because its most visible part checks out 'salient-constraint checking' and treats it as a shortcut, not proper verification. HoVer notes that Refuted vs NotEnoughInfo is often ambiguous for multi-part claims and merges them into Not-Supported. No source I read was specific to cancer-genomics hypothesis labelling, so mapping these conventions onto this task's labels is an analogy. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://aclanthology.org/N18-1074.pdf, https://arxiv.org/html/2011.03088v2, https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2604.10990.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In Ensembl VEP, what defines an 'upstream_gene_variant' (the default distance window), and is it intended to mark promoter regions? ANSWER: upstream_gene_variant (SO:0001631) means only 'a sequence variant located 5' of a gene'. It is a child of intergenic_variant with IMPACT MODIFIER. By default VEP reports upstream/downstream consequences for variants within 5 kb of a transcript (--distance), and it assigns them per transcript, so one variant can be upstream of one isoform and coding in another. The label is positional and does not mark a promoter or regulatory region. An upstream_gene_variant on a single alternative transcript is not, by itself, evidence of a promoter mutation. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer genomics, how are 'promoter mutations' conventionally defined when a recurrent variant is coding under the canonical transcript but lies upstream of an alternative or non-coding isoform's start? ANSWER: Studies define promoter mutations as non-coding variants inside a fixed window around an annotated TSS. Examples: -1 kb/+500 bp around the TSS of canonical GENCODE v19 transcripts (the 2024 promoter-paucity preprint, matching PCAWG); -2 kb/+250 bp around protein-coding TSSs; -2 kb/+200 bp around refTSS-supported TSSs in a melanoma study. The standard examples (TERT C228T/C250T, SDHD) are non-coding. Under canonical-transcript definitions, a recurrent variant that is coding under the canonical transcript would normally be reported as a coding mutation, not a promoter mutation. Only definitions that include every annotated TSS could also count it as a promoter variant of an alternative isoform. No source I read deals with this edge case directly. The exact windows come from search snippets, because the methods text did not come through in the pages I opened. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.06.03.597231v1.full, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4217527/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36535-8, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41416-024-02870-w.

QUESTION: How well do standard whole-exome capture kits cover sequence immediately upstream of first coding exons in GC-rich promoters, and how are recurrent C>T calls in low-complexity GC-rich regions usually checked for artefacts? ANSWER: Coverage is poor. GC-rich promoters near the TSS are systematically under-sampled even in whole cancer genomes (PCAWG coverage analysis). WES covers them badly: the TERT promoter is described as 'poorly covered by the WES' and needed separate targeted sequencing, and GC-rich exome regions are recurrent cold-spots. So the absence of upstream calls in exome data cannot be read as true absence. For artefacts, the usual checks on recurrent C>T calls are: matched-normal and panel-of-normals filtering; strand or read-orientation bias, since FFPE deamination produces C>T/G>A; read depth and alt-read support/VAF; manual IGV review following the somatic variant refinement SOP; and orthogonal validation. Without read counts, a call cannot be checked this way, so it should be treated as unverified, not as confirmed or refuted. The coverage part rests on pages I read. The artefact-check part rests on search snippets only, because the call limit was reached before I could open those pages. HOW SURE: medium. text: FINDING: No single field-wide myeloid threshold exists; conventions are: germline variants show normal VAF near 50% or 100% (Barnell 2018 SOP), while tumour-in-normal contamination shows low normal VAF well below tumour VAF. Caller defaults: MuTect1 rejects if normal has >=2 alt reads or >=3% alt fraction; MuTect2 (GATK3.7) max 1 alt read / 0.03 fraction in normal, often relaxed for deep panels to 0.10 plus AF_tumor > 4x AF_normal; DRAGEN liquid-tumour mode tolerates normal VAF up to 0.2+0.15=0.35 (solid 0.2) and drops artifact_in_normal when normal AF < 0.1x tumour AF. So a CALR call with a few normal reads at low normal VAF (e.g. <~10% and tumour VAF >=4-10x normal) is conventionally consistent with contamination and can still be counted as somatic; normal VAF ~40-60% indicates germline. No conventional germline depth threshold was found beyond caller minimums (MuTect1 normal depth >=8 is a commonly cited default but was not confirmed in pages read). QUESTION: What germline AF and depth thresholds distinguish tumour-in-normal contamination from germline variants in matched myeloid sequencing? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In matched tumour-normal myeloid sequencing, what germline allele fraction and germline depth thresholds are conventionally used to tell tumour-in-normal contamination from a true germline variant? ANSWER: No single myeloid-specific convention exists; the web gives tool defaults and a guiding principle. Principle (Barnell et al. 2018 SOP, Genet Med): a germline variant shows normal-sample VAF near 50% or 100%, with read support in the normal beyond what tumour contamination can explain. Tumour-in-normal contamination instead gives a low normal VAF, well below the tumour VAF. Genomics England (Nat Commun 2024) reports contamination is common in MPN sorted CD3+ T cells and in saliva, which causes true driver hotspots to be wrongly subtracted. Caller thresholds: MuTect1 rejects a call if the normal has >=2 alt reads or >=3% alt fraction (with base-quality sum >20). MuTect2 (GATK 3.7) defaults to at most 1 alt read and a 0.03 fraction in the normal; for deep panels these are commonly relaxed to a 0.10 normal fraction, plus a rule that tumour AF must exceed 4x normal AF (S_AF>0.75). DRAGEN's alt_allele_in_normal filter fires above 0.2 normal VAF plus a contamination tolerance of 0.15 in liquid-tumour mode (0 in solid mode), so the cutoff is 0.35 for haematological samples. DRAGEN also ignores normal artifacts when normal AF < 0.1x tumour AF. Practical reading: a CALR call with a few normal reads at low normal VAF (roughly <10%, and tumour VAF >=4-10x normal VAF) is conventionally treated as contamination and still counted as somatic. A normal VAF of about 40-60% (or about 100%) indicates germline. The pages read give no conventional germline-depth threshold beyond caller minimum-read rules. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3833702/table/T1/, https://best-practices-for-processing-hts-data.readthedocs.io/en/latest/mutect2_pitfalls.html, https://support-docs.illumina.com/SW/DRAGEN_v38/Content/SW/DRAGEN/GPipelinePostSomMat_fDG.htm, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41436-018-0278-z, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-44158-2.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: No single metric is the accepted criterion for 'outperforms'; methodological guidance (Steyerberg et al. 2010 with Vickers, Cook, Pencina, Kattan; Steyerberg et al. 2011) says always report discrimination (C-index) and calibration, add decision-analytic net benefit when the model is meant to guide decisions, and use NRI only as a supplement; the measures can disagree (in the 2011 testicular-cancer example AUC/R2 favoured LDH and AFP while net benefit favoured only HCG), and the guidance does not choose a winner by metric. For nested models, the likelihood-ratio/Wald test of the added predictor is the recommended significance test, and testing the AUC/C difference of nested models on the same data is invalid (Pepe et al. 2013; Demler/Pencina 2013). Non-nested head-to-head comparisons should use the same patients, with a CI for the difference. The TRIPOD pages I could read were truncated, so I found no TRIPOD rule for settling disagreement between metrics. QUESTION: Accepted criteria for claiming a new survival model outperforms an established index, and how guidelines treat disagreement between metrics. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3575184/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3587963/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3625503/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3800241/ ; https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M14-0698

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Apparent (derivation-cohort) performance is systematically optimistic and is not valid evidence of superiority over an externally fixed index such as IPI; the size of the optimism depends on events per variable and on any selection steps, and can be large: in one example, apparent AUC 0.83 fell to 0.76 after bootstrap correction and to 0.57 on external validation (Bleeker et al. 2003). Steyerberg and Harrell (2015) call apparent estimates 'severely optimistic' in small samples, recommend bootstrap validation that repeats all modelling steps including variable selection, and recommend internal-external or external validation for any generalisability claim. AIC penalises only the number of fitted parameters, not data-driven selection of genes or cut-offs (this point is my reasoning, not from a source I read), so an in-sample AIC/C/AUC advantage of a same-cohort genomic model over IPI is weak evidence at most. QUESTION: Typical in-sample optimism of C-index/AIC on the derivation cohort, and whether an apparent advantage counts as evidence of superiority. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5578404/ ; https://www.jclinepi.com/article/S0895-4356(03)00207-5/abstract ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11470385/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In paired pre/post anti-HER2 studies, loss of HER2/ERBB2 amplification is conventionally called a putative acquired-resistance mechanism on descriptive within-patient grounds (amplified at baseline, not amplified at progression after strictly defined acquired resistance), reported as n/N (e.g. 32% of 22 gastric pairs, Pietrantonio 2016; 29% of 48, GASTHER3; 8/25 breast residual tumours, Mittendorf 2009) with no significance test needed for the mechanism claim; formal tests are secondary: Fisher/chi-square vs baseline features, comparison with a cohort not given anti-HER2 therapy (Guarneri 2013 found loss was MORE frequent without anti-HER2, 40% vs 14.7%, p=0.019, so loss is not trastuzumab-specific), and Kaplan-Meier/log-rank or HR vs outcome (Mittendorf RFS p=0.04; Guarneri HR 2.41 p=0.063; GASTHER3 linked loss to no response to second-line T-DM1). A handful of loss events is usually reported as 'one of the mechanisms that may explain resistance' rather than a statistically tested association; no source gives a formal threshold. QUESTION: What framework is conventionally used to claim ERBB2 amplification loss is associated with acquired resistance, and how are a few loss events interpreted? SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.30408 ; https://www.springermedicine.com/loss-of-her2-positivity-after-anti-her2-chemotherapy-in-her2-pos/21403700 ; https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/15/23/7381/75060/Loss-of-HER2-Amplification-Following-Trastuzumab ; https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)36724-9/fulltext ; https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cncr.32809

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: ChainFinder (Baca et al. 2013) builds a graph whose nodes are rearrangement breakpoints (paired-end discordant-read junctions with partner location and orientation) and whose edges are deletion segments from copy number ('deletion bridges'), then keeps closed chains where a multiple-event model is statistically rejected (probability ~1-exp(-mu*D) for adjacent ends at distance D). Both inputs are used, but breakpoint-level SV calls are strictly required; copy-number segments alone cannot link breakpoints across chromosomes, miss balanced/copy-neutral joins, and at most show candidate deletion bridges or deletions at driver genes, which cannot establish or refute chaining. QUESTION: How is chromoplexy detected computationally and can copy number alone detect any part of a chain? SOURCE: https://www.genome.gov/Multimedia/Slides/HGP10Symposium/11_Garraway.pdf ; https://genesdev.cshlp.org/content/27/23/2513/F4.expansion.html ; https://www.cell.com/fulltext/S0092-8674(13)00343-7

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Standard pathway-level 'significantly mutated' tests are background-model tests, not raw-frequency tests. PathScan (Wendl 2011) handles gene length by giving each gene a mutation probability that depends on its length under a random-mutation null. It runs the test separately in each sample using that sample's background rate, then combines the per-sample p-values with Fisher-Lancaster. SLAPenrich (Iorio 2018) also works per sample: the chance that a sample has at least one hit in a pathway is Poisson-based, scaling with the summed exonic block length of the pathway genes times a background rate estimated from the input data. It then tests the number of altered samples. A per-sample-rate x summed-CDS-length model is therefore the accepted standard; a model that ignores gene length is not. QUESTION: How are pathway-level significantly-mutated tests defined and how do they correct for gene length and per-sample rate? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/ https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-25076-6

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In ERG break-apart FISH for prostate cancer, 'rearrangement/translocation with deletion' (Edel) means loss of the 5' ERG signal while 3' ERG is retained, i.e. TMPRSS2-ERG fusion formed by an interstitial deletion of ~3 Mb of chr21q22.2-3 between ERG and TMPRSS2; 'translocation' without deletion (Esplit) means split 5'/3' signals with both retained, i.e. fusion by insertion/translocation that keeps the intervening DNA. The flag encodes the fusion mechanism of one locus only; it does not show whether the rearrangement is chained with others (chromoplexy). QUESTION: What does ERG FISH 'translocation with deletion' mean vs 'translocation'? SOURCE: https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/66/17/8337/526226/TMPRSS2-ERG-Fusion-Associated-Deletions-Provide ; https://www.modernpathology.org/article/S0893-3952(22)02665-5/fulltext ; https://www.nature.com/articles/ncponc0945.pdf ; https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1601467/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In vcf2maf/maf2maf MAFs, FILTER=common_variant tags a variant seen at appreciable frequency in a population database (ExAC, later gnomAD), which makes it a probable germline SNP rather than a somatic mutation. The Van Allen lab re-implementation documents the original rule: tag the variant if at least 10 alleles occur in any ExAC subpopulation, unless it sits at a known somatic site. Current vcf2maf.pl defaults to max_subpop_af 0.0004. Tagging can be turned off with --filter-vcf 0. AACR GENIE uses the filter to remove putative germline SNPs. Such rows are normally excluded from somatic analyses, so they should not count as pathway hits. QUESTION: What does FILTER=common_variant mean in VEP/vcf2maf MAFs and are such rows excluded from somatic analyses? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In paired pre/post-treatment tumor sequencing studies, what statistical framework is conventionally used to claim that loss of a targeted gene amplification is 'associated with' acquired resistance (e.g., frequency vs an untreated reference, link to time to progression), and how are a handful of loss events typically interpreted? ANSWER: The usual approach is descriptive and within-patient. The baseline (pre-treatment) sample is the patient's own control. Loss is called a putative acquired-resistance mechanism when the amplification or positivity is present at baseline and absent at progression, after strictly defined acquired resistance, and it is reported as n/N. Examples: 32% of 22 gastric pairs (Pietrantonio 2016), 14/48 = 29% (GASTHER3), 8/25 residual breast tumours (Mittendorf 2009), and loss of EGFR T790M in 14/36 cases listed alongside other mechanisms (Lee 2020). The mechanism claim itself is not given a significance test. Formal tests are secondary: (a) Fisher/chi-square tests against baseline clinicopathological variables; (b) comparison with a cohort not given anti-HER2 therapy, where Guarneri 2013 found loss MORE often without anti-HER2 therapy (40% vs 14.7%, p=0.019), showing that loss is not specific to trastuzumab and that such a comparison can cut against a selection claim; (c) Kaplan-Meier/log-rank or hazard-ratio links to outcome (Mittendorf: RFS 87.5% vs 50%, p=0.04; Guarneri: HR 2.41, p=0.063, a non-significant 'trend'; GASTHER3: three patients with HER2 loss did not respond to second-line T-DM1). A handful of loss events is typically interpreted as 'one of the mechanisms that may explain' resistance (hypothesis-generating), not as a statistically established association. No source gives a formal threshold for how many events count as an association. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.30408, https://www.springermedicine.com/loss-of-her2-positivity-after-anti-her2-chemotherapy-in-her2-pos/21403700, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/15/23/7381/75060/Loss-of-HER2-Amplification-Following-Trastuzumab, https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)36724-9/fulltext, https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cncr.32809.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How are chromoplexy chains detected computationally (e.g., the ChainFinder approach)? Which inputs are required: paired-end breakpoint coordinates with orientation, copy-number segments, or both? Can copy-number data alone detect any part of a chain? ANSWER: ChainFinder (Baca et al., Cell 2013) builds a graph. Its nodes are rearrangement breakpoints, which are paired-end discordant-read junctions with partner location and orientation. Its edges are chromosomal deletion segments, the 'deletion bridges' taken from copy number. It then searches for closed chains of linked breakpoints in which an independent multiple-event model is statistically rejected: two independent breaks within distance D have probability of about 1-exp(-mu*D), where mu is the per-sample local break density. The method uses both inputs, but breakpoint-level SV calls with partner coordinates and orientation are strictly required. Copy-number segments alone cannot join breakpoints across chromosomes and miss balanced, copy-neutral joins, which are the core of chromoplexy. At most they reveal candidate deletion bridges or deletions at driver genes, which can neither establish nor refute that rearrangements are interdependent. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.genome.gov/Multimedia/Slides/HGP10Symposium/11_Garraway.pdf, https://genesdev.cshlp.org/content/27/23/2513/F4.expansion.html, https://www.cell.com/fulltext/S0092-8674(13)00343-7.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In survival prognostic-model validation, what are the accepted criteria for claiming a new model 'outperforms' an established index: difference in C-index with confidence interval, likelihood-based measures (AIC, LRT), time-dependent AUC, net reclassification, or decision-curve analysis? How do methodological guidelines (e.g., TRIPOD) treat disagreement between these? ANSWER: There is no single accepted criterion. Methodological guidance (Steyerberg, Vickers, Cook, Gerds, Gonen, Pencina, Kattan 2010; Steyerberg et al. 2011) says to always report discrimination (C-index, or time-dependent AUC for survival) and calibration. Decision-analytic net benefit (decision curves) should be added when the model is meant to guide clinical decisions, and NRI is only supplementary. The guidance acknowledges that the measures can disagree. In its worked example, AUC and R2 favoured LDH and AFP, net benefit favoured only HCG, and NRI fell in between. It does not settle such disagreement by ranking metrics. It ties the choice to purpose: for decision support, net benefit at a clinically relevant threshold is preferred over overall AUC. For nested models (IPI vs IPI + genomic), the likelihood-ratio/Wald test of the added predictor is the recommended significance test (Pepe et al. 2013). A separate test of the AUC/C difference between nested models fitted on the same data is redundant and statistically invalid (Demler/Pencina 2013: 'recommend strongly against'). For a non-nested head-to-head comparison (genomic model alone vs IPI alone), compare discrimination on the same patients and give a CI for the paired difference. Ideally this should be done in data independent of model development. The TRIPOD Explanation & Elaboration pages I opened were truncated, so I could not confirm any TRIPOD-specific rule for settling disagreement between metrics. As far as I could see, TRIPOD is a reporting guideline and requires transparent reporting of performance measures rather than setting a superiority criterion. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3575184/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3587963/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3625503/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3800241/, https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M14-0698.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How large is typical in-sample optimism in C-index and AIC for a risk model evaluated on its own derivation cohort, and is an apparent AIC or AUC advantage on the derivation data considered valid evidence of superiority over an externally established index? ANSWER: Performance measured on the derivation data is overestimated, and the amount depends on sample size, events per variable and any data-driven selection. No single 'typical' figure applies. A worked example: apparent AUC 0.83 (n=376), 0.76 after bootstrap optimism correction, and 0.57 on external validation (Bleeker et al. 2003). Steyerberg & Harrell (2015) call apparent estimates in small samples 'severely optimistic'. They require bootstrap internal validation that repeats every modelling step, including variable selection, and recommend internal-external or external validation for any claim about generalisability. Steyerberg et al. (2001) found bootstrapping gives the least biased internal estimate. My inference, not stated in the sources I read: an apparent in-sample AIC, C or AUC advantage of a model derived on the same cohort is not valid evidence that it outperforms an externally fixed index such as IPI, which has no such optimism; at best it is weak, hypothesis-generating evidence unless optimism-corrected or externally validated. On AIC specifically, also my reasoning rather than sourced: it penalises only the number of fitted parameters, not prior selection of genes, groupings or cut-offs on the same data, so it does not remove this optimism. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5578404/, https://www.jclinepi.com/article/S0895-4356(03)00207-5/abstract, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11470385/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer genomics, how are pathway-level 'significantly mutated' tests usually defined (e.g. MutSigCV, OncodriveFM, PathScan, or gene-length-matched permutation)? How do they correct for gene length and for per-sample mutation rate? ANSWER: Standard pathway tests compare what is observed against a background model; they do not use raw frequencies. PathScan (Wendl et al. 2011) gives each gene a mutation probability that depends on its length under a random-mutation null. It tests each sample separately using that sample's background mutation rate and combines the per-sample p-values with Fisher-Lancaster. SLAPenrich (Iorio et al. 2018) also works per sample: the chance that a sample has at least one hit in a pathway is Poisson-based, scaling with the summed exonic block length of the pathway genes times a background rate estimated from the input. It then tests the number of altered samples. So the accepted approach is per-sample rate times summed coding length; a model that ignores gene length departs from the standard. I did not read the MutSigCV or OncodriveFM pages. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-25076-6.

QUESTION: In VEP/vcf2maf-annotated MAF files, what does a FILTER value of 'common_variant' mean, and are such rows normally excluded from somatic mutation analyses? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which genes do standard curated definitions of the ERBB / PI3K-AKT signalling pathway include (e.g. TCGA pan-cancer oncogenic pathway curation versus KEGG ErbB signalling)? ANSWER: No standard defines a single 'ERBB-PI3K' pathway. The TCGA PanCanAtlas curation (Sanchez-Vega et al. 2018, maftools oncogenic_sig_patwhays.tsv) has a 29-gene PI3K pathway: EIF4EBP1, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, AKT1S1, DEPDC5, DEPTOR, INPP4B, MAPKAP1, MLST8, MTOR, NPRL2, NPRL3, PDK1, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PIK3R3, PPP2R1A, PTEN, RHEB, RICTOR, RPTOR, RPS6, RPS6KB1, STK11, TSC1, TSC2. It places EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3 and ERBB4 in RTK-RAS instead. A curated ERBB-PI3K set is therefore ERBB1-4 plus those 29 genes (33 genes). KEGG hsa04012 (ErbB signaling pathway) is much broader: ligands, receptors, MAPK, PI3K/AKT, PLCG, SRC, CBL and others, about 85 genes. My fetch cut off before the KEGG member list, so that count is not checked. The web does not settle which list a given study meant. The TCGA-curated list is the driver-focused standard. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PoisonAlien/maftools/master/inst/extdata/oncogenic_sig_patwhays.tsv, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/, https://rest.kegg.jp/get/hsa04012.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In MSK-IMPACT clinical sequencing, what MSIsensor score thresholds define MSS, indeterminate and MSI-H, and is the convention the same across panel versions? ANSWER: MSS: score < 3; indeterminate: >= 3 and < 10; MSI-H: >= 10. The cutoff was validated against MSI PCR/MMR IHC in 12,288 tumours sequenced on IMPACT 341 (v1), 410 (v2) and 468 (v3) together, and no version-specific thresholds were given, so one convention applies across panels. Most indeterminate scores were MSS by PCR (96.6% in non-CRC/UEC tumours), so treating indeterminate as a sensitivity group is reasonable. The page I read held only the abstract and methods summary, so I could not rule out per-version tuning in the full text, though nothing suggests any. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6130812/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How does OncoKB classify RNF43 G659fs and other frameshifts at mononucleotide repeats, and SMAD4 missense variants outside hotspots, as oncogenic or not? ANSWER: RNF43 G659fs*41 (G659Vfs*41) is curated as Inconclusive for both oncogenicity and biological effect, because the functional data conflict. It is therefore NOT counted as oncogenic, as an explicit exception to the tumour-suppressor truncation rule. Other RNF43 truncating mutations, including R117fs, are not curated individually and fall under 'RNF43 Truncating Mutations', which is Likely Oncogenic; I found no separate rule for repeat-tract frameshifts. SMAD4 is a tumour suppressor: Truncating Mutations (nonsense, frameshift, splice) and Deletion are Likely Oncogenic. SMAD4 missense variants are oncogenic only if individually curated, about 55 alterations in all: e.g. R361C/G/H, D351H/N, G352E, Y353L/S, C324Y, E330A/G/K, R496H, R497H, D537A/E/G/H/V/Y, P130A/S, H132Y, G386D, R420H, D493A/G/H/N, W509R, G510R and R515A/G/I. SMAD4 missense variants that are not curated are unknown/VUS, not oncogenic, because OncoKB assumes oncogenicity only for truncating variants in tumour suppressors. These are current website annotations, and older OncoKB versions may differ. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.oncokb.org/gene/RNF43/G659fs*41, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/RNF43, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4, https://faq.oncokb.org/technical.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: MSK-IMPACT calls whole-gene copy-number changes with an in-house method: GC-normalised tumour/normal coverage log-ratios are segmented by CBS, and a gene counts as gained or lost at fold change >2.0 or <-2.0 with FDR-corrected P<0.05. cBioPortal stores these as discrete values, with +/-2 meaning amplification or deep deletion. These fold changes are not corrected for purity, so the same clonal event gives a smaller fold change in a lower-purity sample. MSK states that depth of coverage and tumour purity affect copy-number calls, and the cBioPortal FAQ warns that because purity and ploidy differ between samples the -2..2 calls can be false positives or negatives. Example: a 2-copy homozygous loss at 50% purity gives only a 2-fold drop, right at the threshold, and at 30% purity a 4-fold amplification gives only about 1.9-fold. A +/-2 call present in a high-purity sample and absent in a low-purity sample of the same patient is therefore often a purity artifact. Check the seg log-ratios and the samples' purities before counting it as new. QUESTION: How are discrete CNA calls derived in targeted-panel pipelines, and how strongly does purity affect reaching +/-2? SOURCE: https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(15)00045-8/fulltext ; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1525157818302447 ; https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In tumour-only calling, even after population-database filtering, residual germline (private) variants are a large share of calls: Jones et al. 2015 (815 tumour-normal pairs) found tumour-only analysis added false positives making up 31% (111-gene panel) to 65% (exome) of reported alterations; rates are higher in non-European ancestry. Standard filters are population databases (dbSNP/1000G/ExAC/gnomAD, AF cutoffs), a panel of normals/virtual normal from unrelated healthy samples (~400 genomes needed to match a matched normal for SNVs), and VAF-based models (germline near 0.5/1.0, e.g. LumosVar). Implication: if patient tumours were called tumour-only and xenografts with a matched normal, germline residue would appear only in T and look like 'lost' mutations; restrict comparisons to variants filtered identically, drop T-only variants with VAF~0.5/1 or present in population databases. QUESTION: Fraction and filtering of residual germline calls in tumour-only vs matched calling. SOURCE: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scitranslmed.aaa7161 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4561496/ ; https://doi.org/10.1186/s12920-017-0296-8

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: There is no standard single test for selection from presence/absence and copy number alone; published PDX studies use comparators as the null: (a) multi-region sampling of the patient tumour, judging T-vs-PDX divergence against within-patient region-to-region divergence (Woo et al. 2021 Nat Genet found PT-PDX CNA differences comparable to multiregion variation, i.e. no evidence of systematic host-driven selection); (b) multiple independent PDX lines from the same tumour/region, where reproducible representation of the same subclone indicates a bottleneck or selection (TRACERx PDX 2024: models often represent a single subclone, a 'genomic bottleneck'); (c) DNA-based rather than expression-inferred CNAs and the same platform/pipeline across samples, because Ben-David 2017's expression-based divergence was largely not reproduced by DNA data; (d) pre-existence of the PDX-dominant clone at low level in the patient tumour (selection of pre-existing minor clones). Without VAF/CCF, presence/absence differences cannot separate selection from sampling or sensitivity; claims need these comparators. QUESTION: Criteria to distinguish engraftment selection from spatial heterogeneity and sensitivity without VAFs. SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-020-00750-6 ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-47547-3 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659952/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Observed tumour/normal ratio R = (p*q + 2(1-p)) / (p*P + 2(1-p)), with purity p, local tumour copy number q and tumour ploidy P. Normal-cell admixture pulls ratios toward 1, so dividing the linear deviation (R-1) by purity is exact only if the tumour is near-diploid (P~2). Dividing log2 ratios by purity is only a small-deviation approximation, because log2 is nonlinear in p. Both fail when ploidy differs between samples: ploidy shifts the log2 baseline, so with whole-genome doubling a single-copy change gives a smaller log2 shift and the zero line means 'average ploidy', not 2 copies. They also fail for subclonal CNAs and when purity is estimated badly. Proper correction estimates purity and ploidy jointly (ABSOLUTE, ASCAT, FACETS, Sequenza, PureCN adjustLogRatio(ratio, purity, ploidy)), ideally using BAF; WGD is common (~37% of cancers). Comparing T and X log2 segments after purity-only scaling can make differences in ploidy or WGD look like copy-number 'selection'. QUESTION: Justification and failure modes of linear purity rescaling of log2 CN ratios. SOURCE: https://www.biostars.org/p/383522/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383288/ ; https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)31355-9/fulltext ; https://bioc-release.r-universe.dev/PureCN/doc/manual.html

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In targeted-panel tumour sequencing pipelines, are mutations seen in one sample of a patient routinely genotyped at the same positions in the patient's other samples (e.g. 'called in another sample' or rescued at low VAF)? What does it mean when a variant appears in only one sample's mutation table? ANSWER: Not routinely, as far as the MSK-IMPACT methods describe. Each tumour is called independently against its matched normal (MuTect/Pindel/SomaticIndelDetector). Hotspot variants need depth >=20x, >=8 alt reads and VAF >=2%; non-hotspot variants need >=10 alt reads and VAF >=5%. The methods papers describe no joint genotyping of one sample's mutations in the patient's other samples. cBioPortal does support a separate 'uncalled' status (PROFILED_WITH_READS_BUT_UNCALLED, i.e. Mutation_Status 'UNCALLED' rows), but I saw this only in a search snippet and did not read the page. A variant listed in only one sample's table therefore means 'not called in the other sample', not 'proven absent'. It may sit below the 2%/5% VAF cutoff, the other sample may have low purity or coverage, or the gene may be off that sample's panel. Teams should check Mutation_Status for UNCALLED rows, drop them before counting, and treat 'new' mutations seen opposite a low-purity sample as uncertain. The web did not fully settle how this specific study's table was assembled. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(15)00045-8/fulltext, https://doctors.anticancer.co.il/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/MSK-IMPACT.pdf, https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/.

ANSWER: MSK-IMPACT computes GC-normalised tumour/normal coverage log-ratios and segments them by CBS. A whole gene counts as gained or lost at fold change >2.0 or <-2.0 with FDR-corrected P<0.05. In cBioPortal, +/-2 means amplification or deep deletion; GISTIC-based studies instead use a fixed low-level threshold (0.1-0.3) and sample-specific high-level thresholds. The fold-change cutoff is not corrected for purity, so purity matters a lot. A 2-copy homozygous loss at 50% purity gives exactly a 2-fold drop, right at the threshold, and anything below 50% purity misses it. At 30% purity, a 4-fold amplification shows only about 1.9-fold. MSK reports that coverage depth and tumour purity affect its CN calls, and the cBioPortal FAQ says purity and ploidy differences make the -2..2 calls prone to false positives and negatives. A +/-2 call present in a high-purity sample and absent in a lower-purity sample of the same patient may well be a purity artifact; check it against the seg log-ratios and the samples' purities. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(15)00045-8/fulltext, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1525157818302447, https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In tumour-only (unmatched) somatic variant calling compared with tumour-normal matched calling, what fraction of calls are typically residual germline variants, and how are they usually filtered? ANSWER: A large share. Jones et al. 2015 studied 815 tumour-normal pairs. Even after filtering against population databases, tumour-only analysis added false positives that made up 31% (111-gene targeted panel) to 65% (exome) of the alterations reported. Most of these were private germline variants. The germline false-positive rate is higher in people of non-European ancestry. Standard filters are: population databases (dbSNP, 1000G, ExAC/gnomAD) with allele-frequency cutoffs; a panel of normals or 'virtual normal' built from unrelated healthy genomes (about 400 genomes are needed to match a matched normal for SNVs, and this removes >96% of the variants a matched normal would remove); and VAF-aware Bayesian callers such as LumosVar, which treat germline VAF near 0.5 (or 1 under LOH) as germline. These callers only work when the tumour is impure enough and sequenced deeply enough. Implication for the teams: if the patient tumours were called tumour-only and the xenografts were called against a matched normal, germline residue would show up only in the tumour and look like 'lost' mutations. Compare only variants that went through the same filters, and treat tumour-only variants with VAF near 0.5 or 1, or listed in population databases, as likely germline. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scitranslmed.aaa7161, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4561496/, https://doi.org/10.1186/s12920-017-0296-8.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In patient-derived xenograft genomics, what criteria are standardly used to distinguish clonal selection at engraftment from spatial sampling heterogeneity and sequencing-sensitivity differences, when variant allele frequencies are unavailable? ANSWER: The web gives no single standard test for this. Published PDX studies instead use comparators as the null. (a) Multi-region sampling of the patient tumour: tumour-vs-PDX divergence is judged against region-to-region divergence within the same patient. Woo et al. 2021 (1,451 samples) found tumour-vs-PDX copy-number differences comparable to multi-region variation, so they saw no evidence of systematic copy-number evolution driven by the mouse host. (b) Several independent PDX models from the same tumour or region: if the same single subclone keeps being represented, that indicates a bottleneck. The 2024 TRACERx PDX study found that models often represent a single tumour subclone, while distinct subclones appear in independent models. (c) DNA-based copy number processed on the same platform and pipeline: Ben-David 2017 reported divergence from expression-inferred copy number, largely through selection of pre-existing minor clones, and this was not reproduced at the same scale with DNA data. (d) Showing that the clone that dominates the PDX already existed at low level in the patient tumour. With only presence/absence and copy-number data and no VAF/CCF, these comparisons cannot by themselves separate selection from sampling or detection sensitivity. The articles I read did not give a formal presence/absence null. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-020-00750-6, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-47547-3, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659952/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How is linear rescaling of log2 copy-number ratios for tumour purity justified, and when does it fail (e.g. different ploidy or whole-genome doubling between samples)? ANSWER: The observed ratio is a mixture: R = (p*q + 2(1-p)) / (p*P + 2(1-p)), where p is purity, q is the local tumour copy number and P is tumour ploidy. This is the standard mixture model behind ABSOLUTE-type methods. I wrote the formula from domain knowledge; none of the pages I read printed it in full. Normal cells pull ratios toward 1, which shrinks the signal. Dividing the linear deviation (R-1) by purity is exact only when the tumour is near-diploid (P about 2). Dividing log2 ratios by purity is only a small-deviation approximation, because log2 is nonlinear in purity. Both fail when ploidy differs between samples: ploidy shifts the log2 baseline, so the zero line means average ploidy rather than 2 copies. After whole-genome doubling a one-copy change gives a smaller log2 shift. Whole-genome doubling is common, at about 37% of cancers. Both also fail for subclonal copy-number changes and when purity is estimated badly. The proper approach estimates purity and ploidy jointly, ideally using B-allele frequency, with tools such as ABSOLUTE, ASCAT, FACETS, Sequenza or PureCN (adjustLogRatio(ratio, purity, ploidy)). Comparing tumour and xenograft log2 segments after purity-only scaling can therefore turn differences in ploidy or whole-genome doubling into apparent 'selection'. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.biostars.org/p/383522/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383288/, https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)31355-9/fulltext, https://bioc-release.r-universe.dev/PureCN/doc/manual.html.

Comparing tumour and xenograft log2 segments after purity-only scaling can therefore turn differences in ploidy or whole-genome doubling into apparent 'selection'. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.biostars.org/p/383522/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383288/, https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(19)31355-9/fulltext, https://bioc-release.r-universe.dev/PureCN/doc/manual.html.

text: REPLY Q1 (timing of post samples): the data have no sample dates. Timing comes only from IMPACT_PRE_POST. HER2_TX_STATUS, HER2_RESPONSE and HER2_TTP are filled on PRE-TX rows only; POST-TX rows are null. Every HER2-amplified pair has a TTP value, so all progressed. The two loss cases are P-0000444 (CR, TTP 25.4) and YJ-her-010 (SD, TTP 7.6); both had initial benefit, so this is acquired resistance. Among retained cases, the POD patients (YJ-her-005, -012, -013) are primary resistance and all kept AMP. Restricting to responders (CR/PR/SD) gives 2/20 losses instead of 2/23. Label unchanged (False).

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (baseline non-amplified): among PRE-TX HER2 IHC/FISH-positive trastuzumab patients, the 4 that are HER2_IMPACT DIPLOID had median TTP 5.8 mo (1 POD, 3 SD, 0 PR/CR). AMP patients had median 11.4-12.9 mo (Mann-Whitney p=0.011). HER2_IMPACT_LR correlates with TTP (Spearman rho 0.41, p=0.003, n=50). A non-amplified tumour population is therefore associated with poor trastuzumab benefit, though this is primary rather than acquired resistance. It supports the False label and does not change the method.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 (TTP losers vs retainers): the two ERBB2-loss patients had TTP 25.4 and 7.6 mo; the 21 retainers had median about 10 mo (Mann-Whitney p=0.62). There is no outcome difference, and with n=2 none could be detected. Following the library convention, the association claim rests on within-patient AMP->non-AMP loss at progression in 2/23 patients (0 gains, 0 changes in untreated multi-sample patients), not on a TTP difference. This weakens strength but does not change the label.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 (excluded trastuzumab patients, P-0000444): 79 patients have trastuzumab in TREATMENT/DETAILS; 26 lack HER2_RESPONSE. Of these, only YJ-her-003 is a HER2-amplified pair (AMP->AMP, already counted). POST-TX-only samples: P-0000570, 0991, 1393, 4046, 4116 and 5618 are IHC/FISH POS and AMP. P-0004407 (5-FU+trastuzumab) is IHC/FISH POS but IMPACT DIPLOID (LR -0.02), a possible further non-amplified case, but it has no baseline. Both loss cases' post samples are also HER2_IHC_OR_FISH NEG, so the loss is confirmed by an independent method. Excluding the site-discordant P-0000444 leaves YJ-her-010 (same-site cardia, truncal mutations shared): 1/22. Label unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (library findings checked against data): (1) Exome coverage of GC-rich promoters is poor, and the MAF agrees: only 50 5'Flank and 16 IGR calls across 20 samples, so the canonical upstream region is effectively not assessed. (2) Promoter windows are usually defined around canonical TSSs; the chr6:44233400 hotspot is coding under the canonical transcript but lies within about 300 bp upstream of the NFKBIE isoform ENST00000477930 start. (3) The VEP upstream_gene_variant label is positional only; the promoter call rests on recurrence and position, not on that label. Conclusion: label stays False with confidence 0.6; the alternative would be Not verifiable, never True.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to purity question: both ERBB2 losses are true copy-number changes. P-0000444 truncal TP53 p.V157_R158del VAF 0.37 pre -> 0.22 post (~44% purity, still ample to detect a high-level amp), ERBB2 LR 4.52 -> 0.10, CDK12 co-amp also lost, new TMEM127 amp. YJ-her-010 TP53 Y234N VAF 0.28 -> 0.81 (post purity higher), FGA 0.07 -> 0.59, ERBB2/CDK12/FGFR2 amps lost and new ALK/DNMT3A/ASXL2 amps appear, i.e. a different clone. The count stays 2/22.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to biopsy-site question: of 22 trastuzumab-treated ERBB2-amp pairs, about 10 are same-site (same SAMPLE_TYPE and SITE_OF_TISSUE_BIOPSY). In those, 1 of 10 lost amplification (YJ-her-010, cardia primary -> cardia primary). P-0000444 is liver met pre -> GEJ primary post, so its loss could come from spatial heterogeneity. That weakens one case but does not remove the same-site loss, so the label stays False and is reported as 2/22 overall, 1/10 same-site.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to post-only question: 8 trastuzumab-treated HER2+ patients have only a POST-TX sample. One (P-0004407, 5-FU+trastuzumab) is HER2_IHC_OR_FISH POS but IMPACT DIPLOID (ERBB2 LR -0.02) at TP53 R175H VAF 0.30 (adequate purity). It is consistent with a post-treatment non-amplified tumor, but there is no baseline to show a loss. No ERBB2 mutations or SVs are in the loss or post-only samples (the only ERBB2 SV is in P-0009872-T02, which stays amplified). Adding these supports the conclusion without changing it.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to TTP/response question: the two loss cases had first-line trastuzumab benefit before progression (TTP 25.4 mo with CR; 7.6 mo with SD), so both fit acquired, not primary, resistance. The 20 retained-amp pairs had median TTP 8.8 mo and 3 had POD as best response. Comparator: the 2 non-trastuzumab ERBB2-amp pairs showed no loss. The label stays False, with descriptive n/N evidence in line with the library finding on convention.
